stories.text: The town's new wealth shows in its Art Nouveau buildings: York Chambers of 1901 and the Midland Counties District Bank of 1903, at 38 and 40 Market Place, and the Carnegie Library on Tamworth Road of 1906, by the same architects, Gorman and Ross. York Chambers and the library are listed Grade II.

stories.text: Nottingham's first station, opened in 1839 by the Midland Counties Railway, stood across Carrington Street; a through station replaced it on this site in 1848. The present building, of red brick and terracotta, was designed by the local architect Albert Edward Lambert and opened on 16 January 1904. Its carriage entrances have Art Nouveau gates of wrought iron. A pair taken down in 1951, made in Leicester in 1904, is now in the Science Museum Group's collection.[^gates]

72578.sum: Nottingham station, briefly known as Nottingham City and for rather longer as Nottingham Midland, is a railway station and tram stop in the city of Nottingham, England. It is the principal railway station of Nottingham. It is also a nodal point on the city's tram system, with a tram stop that was originally called Station Street but is now known as Nottingham Station.

stories.text: The architect Albert Nelson Bromley designed these houses on Newcastle Drive in 1878, and died here in 1934. His buildings in the city include Boots' stores on Pelham Street and Turney Street. He designed many of Boots' shops, in Nottingham and in other towns, and in 1904 the young Thomas Cecil Howitt, later the architect of the Council House, joined his office as an apprentice.

Watson Fothergill designed this shop and warehouse for Furley & Co, provision merchants, in 1896–97; Lloyds Bank has it now. Terracotta panels show the sugar trade, from cutting and boiling the cane to boats and a far eastern market, and the Clinton Street side is faced with glazed Art Nouveau tiles.[^trail]

74724.sum: Furley & Co, on Lower Parliament Street. Today it houses Lloyds Bank, a bank. The building was built in 1896, according to Historic England (via Wikipedia). It is Grade II listed as 12, 14 and 16, Lower Parliament Street.

stories.text: Boots' central store was built on the corner of Pelham Street and High Street to designs by Albert Nelson Bromley: 1902–05 by Historic England's dates, 1903–04 in Wikipedia's list of his works.[^s1] Its shopfront, with curving Art Nouveau panels, has hardly changed and is a rare survivor of its kind.[^he] Historic England suggests it may be the first Art Nouveau shopfront in the country, and that Harrods inspired it.[^hc][^report] Boots left in 1972; Zara trades here now.[^report]
